title: Silence Is Not How Science Advances: Roland Fryer's Call for Courage
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Harriett Janetos uses economist Roland Fryer's Carob Trust Prize for Academic Courage as a springboard to argue that education debates need less ideology and more respect for evidence. She recounts Fryer's claim that scholars who avoid uncomfortable questions about inequality cannot design policies that actually help the groups they say they care about. She highlights his research showing that effective urban schools share strong leadership, high expectations, order and frequent monitoring, and that the Houston effort closed the math achievement gap without first solving poverty. She treats the belief that schools cannot overcome society's ills as an excuse that justifies inaction. Drawing on Robert Pondiscio, Marshall Roberts and Claude Goldenberg, she distinguishes cheap bravery from the professional courage that risks reputation and safety. She closes by urging educators to cool the rhetoric and embrace research-informed pedagogy.
points: Fryer's prize rewards scholars who publish findings that contradict prevailing orthodoxy, on the premise that you cannot design effective policy if you refuse uncomfortable conversations.

The five practices that separated effective charters, namely more instructional time, high-dosage tutoring, frequent teacher feedback, data-driven instruction and high expectations, undercut the claim that poverty must be solved before achievement can rise.
Janetos argues that the belief that schools are powerless is insidious because it excuses poor results and also blocks research-based change.
Courage is not the same as confessing error after the consequences are unavoidable; real professional courage risks reputation and safety.
Lowering the temperature of education debates and accepting science, rather than casting opponents as vermin, is her proposed way to focus on pedagogy that works.
quotes: Roland Fryer is clear and convincing when he says he’s interested in scientific truth, not ideological storytelling.

Fryer himself endured public condemnation—and physical threats—when he published his research about policing that stated findings contradicting the prevailing viewpoint, so he speaks from experience when he says he’s siding with science, not social acceptability.

Fryer deflates the commonly-held belief that poverty dooms educational success and that we can’t improve student outcomes until we’ve improved their societal circumstances. During his three years working with the Houston schools, they were able to close the achievement gap in math.

What is insidious about the belief that schools are powerless to overcome society’s ills is that it is not only used to excuse lack of student progress, but also to justify lack of pursuing educational change at every level based on current research.
Fryer showed us that solving the racial achievement gap is not predicated on solving poverty. It can be done by improving the quality of education.
Roland Fryer has exhibited—and now wants to reward—a different kind of courage, one that can threaten your livelihood and your safety, not just your peace of mind.

While it is true that knowing what research says is not the same thing as successfully translating that research into classroom practice, not knowing what it says doesn’t even provide us the opportunity for a translation to teaching.

Short of that, if we lower the temperature of our discussions by tempering our stance with an acceptance of science, maybe we can leave ideology behind and focus instead on examining and embracing research-informed pedagogy to make our points.
